title: India has no record of when its chief economic advisors served
dek: Without institutional archives or official transition records, researchers could confirm this history only by achieving four-out-of-five agreement among those who lived it.
why: Information density is modest—substantial credits and logistics fill the space—but the middle section on why the state lacks institutional memory is worth hearing.
who: Researchers and policymakers interested in Indian policy history, oral history methodology, the 1991 economic reforms' origins, and subsequent policy evolution.
skip: The lengthy acknowledgments and name lists after 1:41 can be skipped without losing the main argument.

points.h: Two-thirds of Indians have no memory of the license permit system
points.body: Kadambari realized that Prakhar and Shreyas, the most knowledgeable young people in policy circles, couldn't explain how the 1991 reforms happened. This convinced her that almost no one truly knew this history. Over 70% of Indians were born after her, meaning nearly two-thirds never lived under the license permit regime. The project started as an effort to fill this historical gap.

points.h: Four matching accounts out of five became the standard for a historical fact
points.body: Shruti described how many reform details were never written into memoirs or academic papers, only accessible through direct interviews with those who lived them. If four out of five people told the same story, the team treated it as the mainstream account. This is why the project insisted on direct oral histories rather than second and third-hand accounts that lose accuracy.

points.h: No handover tradition meant even chief advisors' tenures went unrecorded
points.body: When Shankar Acharya took office as Chief Economic Advisor, his office had no plaque recording the tenures of his predecessors. He was the tenth; the previous nine had incomplete records, some missing even the exact month. Shreyas realized that even core technical positions in the Finance Ministry had no institutional memory, making oral history not supplementary but essential—the only way to reconstruct this history.

points.h: Indian economic thought survived in obscure committee reports, not university journals
points.body: Niranjan Rajadhyaksha once told Shruti something that never left her: India's university culture and academic journals were weak then, so many officials' real ideas after completing their doctorates never became papers—they stayed scattered across expert committee reports. The team made collecting, scanning, and digitizing these reports core work, even traveling to Nehru Library to photocopy the PC Alexander report. Later they found that even well-known scholar Arvind Panagaria didn't have a copy.

points.h: Six sectors had to move together or the reforms would fail
points.body: Shruti explained why the M document Montek Singh Ahluwalia led was crucial: it didn't handle problems separately, but placed currency, tariffs, license systems, price controls, and fiscal deficits on a single map for coordinated reform. Loosening one constraint made another the new bottleneck. Today's piecemeal state-level land and labor reforms show no results because no one conducts this kind of systems diagnosis anymore.

points.h: One missing photo led to the discovery of three forgotten women officials
points.body: The team found no women in reform-era photographs. Kadambari pursued this gap, finding Bandana Agarwal, Renuka Vishwanathan, and Sindhu Shrikhar in scattered footnotes and memoirs—female IAS officers who drafted industrial policy, managed fiscal expenditure, and advised Chidambaram at the Finance Ministry. Yet literature had almost never systematically recorded their roles.

points.h: Major outlets used the project's research without attribution after Singh's death
points.body: Manmohan Singh refused oral history while alive, fearing his memory would become fiction. After his death, media focused on his premiership's core deals and rural employment law, relegating 1991 reforms to history. But those who lived through the reforms told Shruti that the project had made it "sexy" again. Multiple mainstream outlets borrowed the team's material without acknowledgment.

points.h: Twenty years of state-level reform talent shortage led the project to build supply
points.body: Shruti had heard this complaint in policy circles for two decades: everyone agreed the next reforms must happen at the state level (land, agriculture, energy), yet insisted ‘there are no competent people.’ The team responded by launching the 1991 Fellowship covering ten states with twelve early-career researchers, funded for three years, directly cultivating this previously non-existent talent pool.
